article.title: Thread runout, relief and geometric runout: different drawing requirements
article.metaTitle: Thread Runout vs Relief vs Geometric Runout | ZUFEK
article.description: Distinguish incomplete thread regions, relief grooves and datum-based geometric runout. Define seating clearance, usable engagement and separate acceptance checks.
article.intro: Thread runout can name the incomplete-thread region at the end of a threaded length. Circular or total runout is a separate geometric-tolerance requirement. A drawing should distinguish these meanings, then define any relief groove, usable full thread and seating clearance needed by the assembly.
checklist: Full-thread length and its reference face
Mating chamfer, counterbore or clearance envelope
Separate datum and tolerance for any geometric runout
article.example: Illustrative assembly: a collar must seat against a screw shoulder. Review the collar bore, its entry chamfer and the permitted incomplete-thread region together. A relief may provide clearance, but its section and radius also require design review. A separate geometric-runout callout is considered only if the functional relationship between surfaces requires it. No particular clearance, torque or test result is assumed.
sections: Use three separate terms

An incomplete thread region is where the thread profile is not fully formed near its end. A relief or undercut is a deliberately machined or formed reduced section. Geometric runout controls variation of a specified surface relative to a datum axis. These requirements can coexist on one component, but an axial incomplete-thread length is not a circular-runout tolerance.
Define usable thread before evaluating the transition

Specify the thread system, pitch, tolerance class where applicable and the required usable full-thread length. Identify the reference face and the allowed location of the incomplete region. A visible threaded length can include incomplete profile at an end; it should not be assumed to provide the same usable engagement throughout. Show the mating component when seating depends on this transition.
Check the mating clearance rather than adding a groove by habit

A shoulder, collar, receiving thread or counterbore can interfere with incomplete thread before the intended face seats. Compare the permitted transition envelope with the mating bore, chamfer and axial stack. Where a relief is needed, define its diameter, axial width and transition radius. Review the remaining section with the responsible designer; a clearance groove can also change the local stress condition.
Specify geometric runout only as a separate functional requirement

If the assembly requires control of a surface as the part rotates about a reference axis, identify the controlled surface, datum reference and the selected geometric tolerance. State circular or total runout as appropriate to the drawing system and function. Do not use that datum-based check as a substitute for the permitted axial length of incomplete thread, or impose it merely because the word runout appears in a thread note.
Match each requirement to its own check

A suitable profile or dimensional method can evaluate an accessible incomplete-thread region and relief geometry against the drawing. Thread gauges address their specified thread acceptance and do not automatically verify seating clearance. Geometric runout needs a setup referenced to the required datum axis. A controlled mating-part trial can support seating evaluation, with its revision and limits recorded separately.
Make the quotation and release decision explicit

Ask the supplier to identify any tool-exit allowance, proposed relief or unresolved transition detail before sample approval. Record acceptance in the final supplied condition when treatment can affect the interface. Release the drawing only after usable thread, seating clearance and any independent geometric requirement are unambiguous. The comparison and example describe a review method, not universal dimensions or a certified design.

article.title: A practical guide to shoulder screw drawings
article.metaTitle: A practical guide to shoulder screw drawings
article.description: A shoulder screw drawing needs separate bore-fit, axial-stack, thread and final-surface requirements. Check both tolerance limits before sample approval.
article.intro: A shoulder screw drawing needs separate bore-fit, axial-stack, thread and final-surface requirements. Check both tolerance limits before sample approval.
sections: Define the shoulder

Dimension shoulder diameter and shoulder length independently from thread length. Explain whether the shoulder serves as a locating surface, bearing surface or spacer. The functional role helps identify which features need closer review.
Show how the thread ends

State thread designation and length, and show any relief or transition at the shoulder. Check how the screw seats in the mating assembly. Do not assume the end of the usable thread is identical to the end of the visible thread form.
Review head access and seating

Include head diameter, height and drive configuration. Consider the tool clearance and seating surface in the assembly. A head that fits the drawing may still be inaccessible once neighboring parts are installed.
Communicate functional tolerances

Mark the mating bore relationship and any surface finish requirement that affects motion or fit. Tolerances should be established by the application engineer and confirmed during manufacturing review.
Draw the assembly stack, not only the screw

Show the seating face, moving component, washer or bushing and intended axial clearance. Dimension the shoulder length against this stack. If the shoulder is too short, tightening can clamp the moving part; too long can leave excessive movement. Review the worst permitted stack before approving shoulder length, rather than adjusting it after a binding prototype is received.
Choose datums that match the locating function

Identify the axis and face that locate the part in service. Decide whether shoulder form, runout or another specified relationship affects the mechanism. Listing only outside diameters can leave the functional relationship undefined. Agree how the relationship is checked, particularly if the part is located differently during successive machining operations.
Approve the final supplied surface

Treatment and coating may change the condition used to accept the shoulder. State final limits and coating coverage on the functional surface. The inspection record should distinguish shoulder measurement from thread gauging. A correct thread does not establish that the pivot fits, and a correct external silhouette does not establish surface texture.
Worked review: calculate diametral clearance separately

Assume a finished shoulder diameter of 8.000 ± 0.005 mm and a mating bore of 8.020 ± 0.010 mm. Compare the smallest bore with the largest shoulder, then the largest bore with the smallest shoulder. The resulting 0.005–0.035 mm range is diametral clearance, not radial clearance or an axial gap. These illustrative inputs do not define a standard fit or an approved operating range. The designer still specifies the functional range, temperature basis, datum relationships and final surface condition.

article.title: Five questions before specifying a captive screw
article.metaTitle: Five questions before specifying a captive screw
article.description: Specify a captive screw with its panel, retainer and mating thread. Review installation, released travel and tightened engagement as separate conditions.
article.intro: Specify a captive screw with its panel, retainer and mating thread. Review installation, released travel and tightened engagement as separate conditions.
sections: What retains the screw?
Describe the intended retaining component or geometry. Provide an assembly view and panel details. The screw alone does not establish whether the completed assembly will remain captive.
How much movement is needed?
Show required travel, open position and thread engagement. Explain how the operator installs and releases the fastener, including available access.
What happens during service?
Describe repeated access, vibration, cleaning and exposure conditions. These inputs inform the material, finish and design discussion; they do not replace assembly testing.
How will the assembly be verified?
Define retention and functional acceptance criteria with your engineering team. A dimensional inspection and an assembly test answer different questions.
What should accompany the RFQ?
Include the screw drawing, mating assembly, quantity and any sample photos. Unresolved retention details can be reviewed before a final quotation is issued.
Worked review: release a service panel without losing the screw

For a service-panel design exercise, begin with the intended installation sequence. Show how the screw and retaining part are assembled, which feature prevents escape after release, and where the screw sits once tightened. Check that the available released travel clears the mating thread and permits the panel to open. Then check that the retained hardware does not obstruct seating or reduce the required engagement. Record retention and opening/reassembly as separate checks against the identified panel and retainer revisions.

article.title: How to specify a tamper-resistant screw drive
article.metaTitle: How to specify a tamper-resistant screw drive
article.description: Specify the drive profile, matching tool, finish and installed access together. A bit that fits a loose screw may still fail to engage inside the housing.
article.intro: Specify the drive profile, matching tool, finish and installed access together. A bit that fits a loose screw may still fail to engage inside the housing.
sections: Identify the exact interface

Pin-in six-lobe, five-lobe, Y-type, triangle and two-hole spanner designs are different interfaces. Even visually similar recesses can have incompatible profiles. Supply a controlled drive drawing, recognized interface reference or approved matching tool rather than asking a manufacturer to copy a small photograph.
Define the head and tool access

Head diameter, height and surrounding enclosure affect whether the intended tool can reach the recess. Show the assembled condition, including any counterbore or nearby wall. A usable loose screw can become difficult to service after it is installed inside the product.
Review pin and recess features

For a center-pin drive, include the pin geometry, recess depth and relevant edge condition. Forming and secondary machining offer different ways to create these details. Inspect the functional tool engagement as well as the external head dimensions; a recess can look correct while fitting poorly.
Separate access resistance from joint performance

A special drive can discourage casual removal, but it does not make a joint impossible to open. Material, thread engagement and the tightening method still determine the mechanical connection. Define service access, installation torque requirements and the intended tool-control arrangement independently.
Worked review: distinguish a tool-fit issue from an access issue

Consider a pin-in screw in a recessed cover. First compare the finished recess with the identified service bit outside the housing. Next review the same bit in the installed position, including its holder and approach space. If engagement is satisfactory outside but restricted inside, review the access envelope before changing the drive profile. If the bit cannot seat in either position, review the recess, pin, bit and final finish together. Record which interface changed and repeat the affected check with the same controlled tool reference.
article.example: For an enclosure fastener, supply the enclosure recess and service-tool outline alongside the screw drawing. This allows the quotation review to consider drive engagement and access together before tooling is selected.

article.title: Hollow screw bores: the details an RFQ should include
article.metaTitle: Hollow screw bores: the details an RFQ should include
article.description: Specify the complete bore, minimum remaining wall, internal edges and acceptance method. Use thread-root geometry and bore offset in the section review.
article.intro: Specify the complete bore, minimum remaining wall, internal edges and acceptance method. Use thread-root geometry and bore offset in the section review.
sections: Describe the entire passage

Identify whether the hole is through, blind, stepped or connected to a side passage. Dimension each section and its axial position. A single opening diameter does not define an internal path, and a photograph cannot establish hidden counterbores or restrictions.
Review wall thickness with the thread

The bore and external thread share the same material section. Show their relationship through the thinnest region and identify any concentricity or position requirement. Manufacturing review needs the actual geometry; an outside diameter alone is not sufficient to evaluate a hollow threaded feature.
State edge and cleanliness requirements

Drilling can leave burrs at hole exits and intersections. Specify which edges must be broken and how internal burrs will be accepted. If the part carries fluid, adhesive or a wire, explain the relevant contamination, surface-damage or blockage concern rather than relying on a generic clean note.
Define functional tests separately

A continuous bore does not itself prove pressure capability, leak tightness or unrestricted flow in an assembly. State any test medium, fixture arrangement and acceptance method that the application requires. These conditions should be agreed before sampling so manufacturing and inspection can be quoted together.
Worked review: include bore offset in the wall calculation

For an illustrative circular section, take a lower-limit thread-root envelope diameter of 6.00 mm, an upper-limit bore diameter of 3.00 mm and a maximum radial bore-centre offset of 0.20 mm. The minimum remaining wall in that section is (6.00 − 3.00) ÷ 2 − 0.20 = 1.30 mm. The offset is a radial distance here, not a diametral position-tolerance callout. This calculation does not cover cross-hole intersections, other local sections or load capacity. Derive the actual inputs from the controlled geometry and its tolerance limits.
checklist: Hole exit and intersection burr limits
article.example: For a screw used as a cable passage, show the cable envelope and the edges it contacts. For a fluid passage, describe the intended sealing interface separately from the through hole.

article.title: Designing the bearing face of a custom flange screw
article.metaTitle: Designing the bearing face of a custom flange screw
article.description: Match the flange bearing face to the actual supporting surface. Compare the contact footprint, finish and grip length before replacing a separate washer.
article.intro: Match the flange bearing face to the actual supporting surface. Compare the contact footprint, finish and grip length before replacing a separate washer.
sections: Start with the mating surface

Identify the material beneath the flange and the available contact area. A soft panel, coated bracket and rigid machined seat respond differently. Show holes, slots and nearby edges so the bearing footprint can be reviewed against the real supporting surface.
Dimension the flange as a functional feature

Specify diameter, thickness and the transition beneath the head. Include flatness or surface requirements when they affect contact. Thin flanges and large overhangs should not be assumed to distribute load uniformly; their behavior needs review with the intended connection and material condition.
Choose the face condition deliberately

Plain, textured and serrated bearing faces are not interchangeable. A serration may change the contact behavior and affect a coating or soft surface. Explain whether the priority is appearance, resistance to movement, contact pressure or another function, then agree the relevant acceptance checks.
Include the finish and tightening conditions

Coating thickness and friction can influence the assembled joint. Treat the flange face and threads as specified surfaces, not simply parts of an overall color requirement. Any comparison with a washer assembly should consider the complete joint rather than the number of handled components.
Worked review: compare an integral flange with a washer assembly

For a coated slotted bracket, compare the existing head-and-washer arrangement with the proposed integral flange on the same bracket drawing. Identify the supporting surface left around the slot and the areas that must remain clear. Review flange or washer overhang, the under-head transition and permissible coating marks. Account for the washer thickness when comparing grip length and usable engagement. Keep the assembly method and acceptance criteria explicit; fewer loose components do not establish equivalent bearing behavior or retained clamp load.
article.example: When replacing a loose washer with an integral flange, provide both assembly drawings. The review should compare the supporting footprint and seating condition before treating the two arrangements as equivalent.

article.title: Cone, flat, dog or cup: choosing a set-screw tip
article.metaTitle: Cone, flat, dog or cup: choosing a set-screw tip
article.description: Choose a set-screw point by its contact with the mating part. Define allowable marking, adjustment and retention, then verify the complete joint.
article.intro: Choose a set-screw point by its contact with the mating part. Define allowable marking, adjustment and retention, then verify the complete joint.
sections: Choose the contact mechanism first

A point name describes geometry, not the holding capacity of the completed joint. Use the comparison below to shortlist a contact mechanism. Then provide the mating material and hardness, the prepared flat, recess or hole, and the intended adjustment and release procedure. A flat point is worth reviewing when a sharp biting edge is undesirable; it does not guarantee a mark-free shaft. A cone or cup can indent the mating surface. A dog point needs a defined mating hole or slot.
Work through an adjustable-stop example

Consider a fixture stop that is reset between jobs and contacts a finished pad. This is a design exercise, not a delivered customer case. First decide whether indentation is acceptable. If it is not, review broad-face contact and the pad material before selecting a point. Check alignment throughout the adjustment travel: a nominally flat end can contact on an edge if the screw approaches at an angle.
Separate location from frictional clamping

If a cylindrical dog enters a hole, show its projection and the available hole depth. Decide whether that extension locates the part, guides its movement or transmits a defined load. Provide clearance for the intended motion and check the installation sequence. Do not assume that an extension in a hole is an approved shear connection or that tightening the screw establishes the required retention by itself.
Release a point and a verification plan

Show the thread, drive access, overall length, point dimensions, final material condition and surface treatment on the controlled drawing. Agree installation requirements and a functional trial on a representative mating component. Record permitted marking and the behavior after the required adjustment or service sequence. No general torque or holding-force value is supplied here: those depend on the actual joint.
Write a repeat-adjustment acceptance record

For the fixture-stop exercise, define the starting setting, allowed contact mark and adjustment/service sequence before the trial. Check contact at both ends of travel and after returning to the starting setting. Record whether each result is a visual assessment, a dimensional reading or a functional observation. If the pad or point geometry changes, compare against the same criteria rather than reusing the old result. This creates an acceptance record; it does not establish a universal tightening torque or holding force.
checklist: Mating surface, recess or hole drawing
Thread engagement, access and installation requirements
article.example: Illustrative review outcome: a repeat-adjusted stop uses a prepared contact pad and a defined end face. The trial checks contact throughout travel, visible marking and retention of the setting under the agreed conditions. Dimensions, material, torque and loads remain project inputs; no test result is claimed.
